hook: Stores use one psychology trick on you every single day.

blocks.narration: Stores use one psychology trick on you every single day. It is called anchoring, and it changes what feels like a good price.
blocks.visual: Minimal surreal 3D clay figure staring at a giant price tag shaped like an anchor, soft pastel studio light

blocks.narration: In nineteen seventy-four, psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman ran a now famous experiment with a rigged wheel of fortune.
blocks.visual: A clay wheel of fortune spins on a pastel stage

blocks.narration: The wheel secretly landed only on ten or sixty-five. Then people estimated what percentage of African nations were in the United Nations.
blocks.visual: The wheel stops on one number, then a clay globe appears with a question mark

blocks.narration: People who saw sixty-five gave much higher estimates than those who saw ten, even though the wheel was obviously random.
blocks.visual: Two clay figures hold up signs, one much taller than the other

blocks.narration: That first number becomes an anchor. Your brain adjusts away from it, but usually not nearly far enough to be accurate.
blocks.visual: A clay boat tied to an anchor drifts a little but cannot move far

blocks.narration: Stores use this constantly. A was price of two hundred dollars makes ninety-nine feel like a steal, whatever the item is worth.
blocks.visual: A clay price tag flips from a crossed-out big number to a smaller glowing one

blocks.narration: It shows up in salary talks, car buying, and real estate too. Whoever names the first number often shapes the whole negotiation.
blocks.visual: Two clay figures across a table, one placing a large number card down first

blocks.narration: Before you buy, ask what you would pay with no anchor at all. Follow for more psychology that saves you money.
blocks.visual: The clay figure cuts the anchor rope and floats freely as the camera pulls back

cta: Follow for more psychology that saves you money.

captions.hook_line: Stores use this psychology trick on you every single day ⚓
captions.body: In a classic 1974 study, Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to land on 10 or 65; people who saw 65 gave much higher estimates to an unrelated question. 'Compare at' prices and opening offers work the same way.
